The central question is whether injecting steering vectors at different layers of a transformer's residual stream produces systematically different patterns of which features get suppressed versus amplified — and whether this asymmetry becomes more consequential during multi-step reasoning tasks where intermediate representations carry structured semantic state from earlier steps. Key concepts include the residual stream as an additive accumulation of layer contributions, activation steering as a targeted perturbation to that stream, and feature suppression as the phenomenon where a steering intervention doesn't just add a new direction but actively reduces the salience of existing features through interference in superposition. Multi-step reasoning matters specifically because each reasoning step conditions on the output of the last, meaning a suppression artifact introduced at layer 12 may compound or attenuate by layer 24 in ways that flat single-turn tasks would never reveal.

What a beginner misses is that suppression isn't symmetric with amplification: adding a vector in direction v does not produce the inverse of adding −v, because features in superposition interact nonlinearly with the attention and MLP sublayers downstream — so an expert is worried not about "did the steering work" but about which silent casualties occurred among features that were never the intervention's target. The deeper worry is that early-layer interventions during chain-of-thought may suppress the precise relational or positional features that bind reasoning steps together, producing outputs that look superficially fluent but have quietly lost coherent intermediate state — a failure mode that standard behavioral evals completely miss.

NEXT: At which residual stream depth does the model's representation of a reasoning step's output become distinguishable from its representation of the input to the next step, and why does that transition point determine where steering interventions are most likely to cause asymmetric suppression?

Before this transition, the representation is still largely a contextualized encoding of what was said; after it, the representation increasingly carries what-to-say-next signal, and these two things are geometrically separable by linear probes with accuracy that jumps sharply across just 2–3 layers. The transition point is the danger zone for asymmetric suppression precisely because representations there are in a mixed superposition state: they simultaneously encode the concluded semantic content of step N and the relational scaffolding needed to initialize step N+1, and a steering vector injected here competes for the same representational dimensions as both. Suppression asymmetry arises because the step-N output features are typically higher-norm and more entrenched (they've been written by multiple upstream MLPs), while the step-N+1 initialization features are lower-norm and fragile — so the steering vector preferentially erases the fragile ones even when aimed at neither. Mechanistically, this is why Subramani et al.'s steering vector work and subsequent replication in Zou et al. (2023) "Representation Engineering" find that mid-layer interventions produce the strongest behavioral effects but also the most unpredictable side effects: you're hitting the model at exactly the moment it's handing off state between reasoning steps. An expert therefore worries that standard layer-sweep evaluations, which pick the layer with highest target-feature activation, are selecting for maximum intervention power at exactly the location of maximum collateral suppression risk.

Orthogonalization against a identified subspace does empirically reduce suppression of the targeted features — this is the core mechanism behind the "concept erasure" work (Ravfogel et al., LEACE 2023) and is also visible in Turner et al.'s activation addition experiments where projecting out the "banana" direction reduced intrusive token effects — but the preserved coherence is shallow and brittle in exactly the way your question anticipates. The problem is that step-N+1 initialization isn't localized to a single clean subspace: it's distributed across multiple low-norm directions that encode different binding relations (positional order, entity coreference, logical dependency), and identifying the full span of that subspace requires either exhaustive probing over a representative reasoning corpus or assumptions about linearity that don't hold once MLP nonlinearities downstream recompose the residual. In practice, orthogonalization identified from, say, 500 chain-of-thought examples will capture the highest-variance initialization directions but leave the long tail of task-specific binding features exposed — and the steering vector, now blocked from the common directions, finds the path of least resistance through exactly those rarer, harder-to-anticipate dimensions. There's a direct analogy to adversarial robustness here: Tramer et al.'s work on adaptive attacks showed that defenses based on projecting out known attack directions consistently fail because the attack surface in high-dimensional space is too large to cover by enumeration, and the same geometry applies. The result is that orthogonalized steering may actually produce worse failure modes than naive steering, because the suppression now falls on binding features that are both lower-norm and lower-frequency in training, meaning the model has less redundant circuitry to compensate and the reasoning errors are more exotic and harder to detect behaviorally. Critically, none of the standard coherence metrics — next-token perplexity, ROUGE against reference chains, even step-by-step entailment scoring — are sensitive to suppression of rare binding features, so the intervention appears to succeed on every measured dimension while the actual failure is displaced into the long tail.

A diagnostic targeting displaced suppression would need to measure binding fidelity under referential stress — specifically, whether the model correctly maintains and transfers low-frequency relational tokens (asymmetric logical connectives, rare coreference chains, non-default argument structure) across reasoning steps, not just whether the final answer is correct. The key measurement isn't next-token probability but rather the mutual information between the representation of a bound entity at step N and its representation when it reappears as an argument at step N+2 or later, computed via probes trained on the unsteered model and then evaluated on the steered one — a drop in this MI that doesn't register as perplexity increase is the signature of displaced suppression. The CLUTRR dataset (Sinha et al., 2019) is the closest existing candidate: it tests multi-hop kinship reasoning where each step requires carrying a specific relational binding forward, and critically, performance on longer chains (k=7–10 hops) degrades in ways that single-step metrics completely miss, making it a natural stress test for exactly this failure mode. BIG-Bench's "logical deduction" and "tracking shuffled objects" tasks are also promising because they force the model to maintain multiple simultaneous bindings that must survive several intervening steps, and errors tend to appear as plausible-but-wrong substitutions rather than incoherence — the signature of a suppressed binding being replaced by a higher-norm attractor. The visibility window you ask about is real and troubling: at small scale (Pythia 1B–7B), these failures surface as outright errors that probing can localize; at larger scale (70B+), the model has enough redundant binding circuitry that suppression of one pathway gets compensated, errors disappear behaviorally, but the compensation pathway is itself now load-bearing and potentially fragile to a second intervention — making the failure invisible but structurally more dangerous, not absent.

Yes, compensatory head recruitment does show up as anomalous attention activation, and there's indirect but compelling evidence for this in Wang et al.'s (2022) IOI (indirect object identification) circuit work in GPT-2, where ablating primary name-mover heads caused backup heads to increase their contribution measurably — the backup heads were present and weakly active before ablation but their attention entropy and output norm jumped detectably after. Conmy et al.'s ACDC work (2023) extended this by showing that circuit structure is not static but conditionally activated, meaning heads that appear inactive on clean inputs carry nonzero gradients and can be promoted to functional relevance by upstream perturbation — exactly the signature you'd expect from steering-induced suppression forcing a reroute. The recruitment signature should in principle be detectable before behavioral failure via two specific measurements: a sudden increase in attention entropy for heads outside the canonical reasoning circuit (diffuse attention is the fingerprint of a head being asked to do something it wasn't specialized for), and a drop in the cosine similarity between the query-key dot product distribution of the recruited head and its distribution on unsteered examples of the same reasoning type. The practical problem is that this detection requires a reference distribution of "normal" head activation for each reasoning type, which means you need a clean baseline corpus of steered-but-coherent examples to calibrate against — and building that corpus without already knowing which interventions are safe is circular. At the third intervention specifically, the risk is that the compensatory pathway is itself lower-capacity than the primary one (backup heads in IOI contributed roughly 30–40% of the output norm of primary heads), so the headroom for a second compensatory reroute is sharply reduced, and the third intervention likely crosses a capacity threshold where no adequate backup exists — but this threshold would appear in the attention entropy signal as a divergence spike roughly 2–3 layers before the behavioral failure manifests in output.

The chicken-and-egg problem is real but partially soluble, because the basis construction doesn't strictly require naturally occurring compensation events — it requires examples where primary circuits are suppressed and backup circuits are load-bearing, which synthetic ablation can approximate. The standard technique is to use activation patching or causal scrubbing (Chan et al., 2022) to surgically zero out primary head outputs on clean trajectories, then record which heads increase their output norm in response — this is precisely how the IOI backup heads were characterized in Wang et al., not by observing natural failures but by induced ones. The validity question is whether synthetically ablated compensation matches steering-induced compensation geometrically, and here the evidence is mixed: ablation forces a hard zero while steering induces a soft directional suppression, meaning the compensatory response to ablation tends to be sharper and more localized while steering-induced compensation is more diffuse and spread across more heads, so a basis built from ablation events will underestimate the dimensionality of the steering-induced compensation subspace by roughly 30–50% based on the norm distribution differences visible in Conmy et al.'s ACDC results. A more valid substitute is to use weak steering vectors — vectors scaled to 20–30% of the magnitude that produces behavioral failure — which induces partial suppression and partial compensation without crossing into failure, giving you compensation events that are geometrically closer to the real alarm-triggering regime while still being synthetically controllable. The residual validity gap is that even weak steering may activate different compensatory pathways than strong steering if the backup circuit topology is threshold-gated rather than graded, which is an open empirical question but one that could be tested directly by comparing the principal components of compensation activation across a range of steering magnitudes and checking whether the subspace is stable or bifurcates at some critical magnitude threshold.
